### GLOSSARY

# What is a hybrid workplace?

A hybrid workplace is a way of working where employees split their time between the office and somewhere else, usually home. Instead of everyone being in the building five days a week, people come in on certain days, for specific reasons (like meetings or team work), and the office is designed around that rhythm. Done well, it gives people flexibility without losing the energy of being together.

## What is a hybrid workplace?

Think of the traditional office as a place you go to because that’s where work happens. A hybrid workplace flips that. Work can happen anywhere, so the office has a different job: it’s where people come to collaborate, connect, learn from each other, and do the things that are just better in person.

That change touches almost everything. Desks aren’t permanently “yours” anymore. Meeting rooms need to work for people in the room and people on a screen. Someone has to figure out which days are busy, which are quiet, and whether the space you’re paying for matches the way people use it.

The technology that holds it together is covered in our guide to [**hybrid office software**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/hybrid-office-software/), and the bigger discipline behind it is [**workplace management**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/workplace-management/).

### Did you know?

According to [**Gallup's 2026 data**](https://www.gallup.com/401384/indicator-hybrid-work.aspx), about half of US employees in remote-capable jobs (52% as of May 2026) work a hybrid schedule, a number that has held steady since 2022. In other words, the hybrid workplace isn't a pandemic leftover. It's settled in.

## How does it work?

Every hybrid workplace runs on the same basic loop. The company sets expectations about when people come in. Employees plan their week around them, reserve a desk or a room, and head in. Once there, they check in, find their team, and get on with their work. In the background, the people running the space watch what’s happening and adjust.

The space itself is built to support that loop. Walk into a well-designed hybrid workplace and you’ll usually notice:

- **Shared desks.** People book what they need for the day instead of owning a fixed spot.

- **Team neighborhoods.** Zones for specific teams or projects, so people who work together sit together.

- **More room to collaborate.** Heads-down work works well in a home office. Workshops and brainstorms don’t.

- **Rooms built for mixed groups.** Screens and cameras make remote colleagues part of the conversation, not an afterthought.

- **Screens and a friendly front door.** Screens show which rooms are free and where to find your team, and an easy check-in welcomes guests even when their host is working from home.

What makes or breaks it is how smooth the loop feels. If booking a desk takes five clicks, finding your team takes a text thread, and nobody knows who’s in on Thursday, people stop planning and start guessing. The best hybrid workplaces make the plan obvious and the logistics practically invisible.

## Common hybrid workplace models

There’s no single “right” way to do hybrid. Most companies land on one of these, or a mix:

- **Minimum days.** Everyone comes in on at least a set number of days a week (two or three is common), and picks which ones. It’s simple and flexible, but attendance can spread out unevenly.

- **Specific days.** The company sets the days, such as Tuesday through Thursday. Everyone is in at the same time, so teams can plan meetings and workshops around those days. The catch is that the office is packed on those days and quiet the rest of the week.

- **Team anchor days.** Each team picks shared days to be in together, so collaboration is planned rather than accidental.

- **Employee choice.** People decide when to come in based on what they’re working on. It’s the most flexible, and the hardest type of hybrid work to plan space for.

- **Office as a hub.** The default is remote, and the office is for key moments such as workshops, onboarding, and big meetings.

## Hybrid workplace by the numbers

### 87% of employees face challenges collaborating in hybrid or remote settings

Hybrid is popular, but it isn’t automatically easy. The biggest hurdle people named was inconsistent communication across channels (44%), followed by limited visibility into colleagues’ schedules (29%) and not knowing when colleagues will be in the office (23%), according to [**Appspace 2026 workplace trends & insights report**](https://www.appspace.com/workplace-trends-report/). In other words, the problem is usually coordination, not commitment, and it’s fixable with a shared plan and clear information.

### 90% say hybrid policies are fair when the team decides together, versus 73% when leadership decides

Who sets the rules matters almost as much as what the rules are. Yet [**Gallup**](https://www.gallup.com/401384/indicator-hybrid-work.aspx) found only 11% of employees were in a team that sets its own hybrid policy.

### The average company asks for about 2.8 office days a week

[**The Flex Index**](https://www.lse.ac.uk/management/assets/documents/research/flex-index-reports/Flex-Report-Q2-2025.pdf), which tracks workplace policies across thousands of US companies, put the average required office time at roughly 2.8 days a week in mid-2025, up from about 2.5 a year earlier. Among companies that require a set number of days, three is now the most common request. It’s a useful benchmark when you’re deciding what’s reasonable for your own team.

## Benefits

Done well, a hybrid workplace works for the people in it and the business behind it.

- **People get flexibility.** Fewer commutes and more control over how the day goes. Gallup reports that six in ten remote-capable employees say hybrid is their ideal setup, versus just 6% who prefer to be fully on-site.

- **The office becomes more purposeful.** When people choose to come in, they tend to come in for something: a project kickoff, a team lunch, a conversation that’s better face to face.

- **Smarter use of space.** Understanding how rooms and desks are used lets you right-size the footprint instead of paying for seats that sit empty.

- **A wider talent pool.** Flexibility makes it easier to hire and keep people who can’t or won’t commute five days a week.

- **Better collaboration when it counts.** Planned in-person days, like team anchor days, put the right people in the same room at the same time.

## How to set up a hybrid workplace: Best practices

If you’re building or rebuilding one, here’s a practical order of operations.

1. **Start with what’s happening.** Look at how people use the space today: which days are busy, which rooms get booked, which desks sit idle. If you don’t have data yet, start collecting it now.

2. **Choose a model, and involve the people who’ll live with it.** Pick the days-in-office approach that fits your work, and let teams have a say. They’ll be far more likely to stick with a policy they helped shape.

3. **Redesign the space around how people work.** Shift from rows of fixed desks to shared desks, team neighborhoods, and more places to collaborate. Not sure where to begin? Start with the rooms people complain about most.

4. **Make the logistics effortless.** People should be able to book a desk, find a colleague, and check in a guest in seconds. That’s where good [**space reservation**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/space-reservation/) and [**visitor management**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/visitor-management/) come in.

5. **Keep everyone in the loop, in the building or not.** Announcements shouldn’t depend on who happened to be near the whiteboard. Take a look at our guide to [**internal communications**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/internal-communications/).

6. **Review and adjust.** Check the data regularly and tweak the policy, the layout, and the tools. A hybrid workplace is never really “finished.”

7. **Ask for feedback and act on it.** The people using the space every week will spot what isn’t working long before a report does.

## Challenges to watch for – and how to fix them

Every hybrid workplace runs into a few predictable bumps.

- **Mandates that don’t match behavior.** Setting office-day requirements doesn’t automatically change attendance. If the space is hard to use, expect pushback. Fix it by making the office easier and more useful.

- **Crowded days vs. empty ones.** If demand clusters on certain days, spread it out with team schedules, booking rules, and visibility into what’s busy.

- **Not knowing who’s in.** It’s hard to collaborate when you can’t tell which days your team is around. A shared view of who’s coming in solves most of this.

- **A two-tier experience.** People in the room hear things first and have the best seat at the table. Run meetings so remote colleagues have an equal voice and share updates in writing.

- **Fragmented tools.** If booking, check-in, and communications live in separate systems, nobody has the full picture. Consolidating helps, and our guide to [**hybrid office software**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/hybrid-office-software/) shows what that looks like.

## Industry use cases – how it works in practice

### Nonprofit / association: American Chemical Society

When the American Chemical Society moved its Washington, DC headquarters to a hybrid model, the traditional office layout no longer matched how people showed up. ACS switched to desk hoteling so employees could reserve a workspace only when they needed one, then layered in room reservations, digital signage, wayfinding, and employee communications on top.

What started as a search for a simple booking tool turned into a single system that keeps a 150-year-old scientific society’s hybrid workforce connected and oriented, whether they’re in the building or not.

Read the full customer story: [**How the American Chemical Society created a smarter, more connected hybrid workplace**](https://www.appspace.com/resources/case-studies/c/acs-hybrid-workplace-strategy-cs)

### Banking: a multi-branch financial institution

A bank with both a corporate headquarters and branch locations needed one system to manage two very different hybrid challenges at once: flexible desk and room use at HQ, and consistent, up-to-date signage across its branches.

By running space management and digital signage through the same platform, the bank could keep branch content current and support hybrid scheduling at headquarters without stitching together separate tools for each side of the business.

Read the full customer story: [**How a financial firm managed space and communication for hybrid work**](https://www.appspace.com/resources/case-studies/c/branch-signage-banking-cs)

## Technology and tools

You don’t need every tool on day one. Start with the biggest friction in your workplace today and add from there. Whatever you pick, a few questions are worth asking first:

- **Will people use it?** The best tool is the one that takes seconds to use. Look for booking and check-in that work from a phone, a desktop, or a screen on the wall.

- **Does it fit what you already use?** If your teams live in Outlook, Google Calendar, Teams, or Slack, the tools should plug into them instead of asking people to learn a new routine.

- **Can it handle your mix of people and spaces?** Think desks, meeting rooms, parking, visitors, and colleagues who rarely come in. A tool that only handles one of these leaves gaps.

- **Can you see what’s working?** You’ll want usage data you can act on, such as busy days, unused rooms, and visitor numbers, without building reports by hand.

## Hybrid workplace vs. related terms: what’s the difference?

Plenty of terms get tossed around in this space. Here’s how they compare.

### Hybrid workplace vs. a fully remote company

Fully remote teams don’t rely on a shared office at all. A hybrid workplace keeps a physical space as part of the plan, which means someone has to manage it.

### Hybrid workplace vs.a traditional office

A traditional office assumes everyone is present every day, so space is assigned and fixed. A hybrid workplace assumes attendance varies and plans space and tools around that.

### Hybrid workplace vs. hot desking

[**Hot desking**](http://www.appspace.com/glossary/hot-desking) is one way to run a hybrid workplace (first-come, first-served desks). A hybrid workplace is the broader setup.

### Hybrid workplace vs. hybrid office software

A hybrid workplace is the way of working and the space it happens in. [**Hybrid office software**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/hybrid-office-software/) is the set of tools that helps you run it, from booking desks to keeping remote and in-office teams on the same page.

### Hybrid workplace vs. workplace management

[**Workplace management**](https://www.appspace.com/glossary/workplace-management/) covers everything that keeps a workplace running. Managing a hybrid workplace is one of its biggest jobs today.

## Frequently asked questions

### **In a hybrid workplace, how many days a week should people be in the office?**

There’s no universal answer. The right number depends on your work, your teams, and what you want the office to be used for. Involving teams in the decision tends to help.

### **Do you need assigned desks in a hybrid workplace?**

Not usually. Most hybrid workplaces use shared desks that people reserve ahead of time (often called desk hoteling) or grab on arrival (hot desking). Many also create team neighborhoods so people who work together can sit together.

### **Does a hybrid workplace mean less office space?**

Sometimes, but not automatically. Peak-day attendance can still be high, so many companies focus on making better use of space and improving quality, instead of shrinking it dramatically. Real usage data is the best guide.
